title: Hakuin's cure
hookLine: Hakuin's "Zen sickness" and the butter-ball meditation he learned from a hermit

cards: Hakuin, the same Zen teacher from yesterday's story, wrote about a time when practice made him sick. As a young monk he threw himself at it, sitting, straining, pushing day and night.
Then, in his own telling, his body turned on him. His head burned, his legs felt like ice, his ears rang, he was anxious and couldn't rest, and doctors couldn't help. He called it Zen sickness.
So he went looking for a hermit in the mountains.

teach.b: The account comes from a short work of Hakuin's, often called Idle Talk on a Night Boat. First, the hermit. Hakuin says he climbed into the hills near Kyoto to find a recluse named Hakuyu, who lived in a cave.
Hakuyu told him the trouble wasn't too little practice. He'd pushed all his energy up into his head, and it needed to come down. Second, settling low.

teach.h: BRING IT DOWN TO THE BELLY.
teach.b: Hakuyu taught him to bring attention and breath down into the lower belly, below the navel, and rest it there, especially at night, lying down. Third, the butter, the image at the center of it.
Imagine a lump of soft, fragrant butter resting on the crown of your head.

teach.h: THE BUTTER MELTS, HEAD TO FEET.
teach.b: Slowly it warms and melts, trickling down over the head, face and shoulders, through the chest and belly, down the back and legs to the soles of the feet, soothing everything it touches. Fourth, the result.
In Hakuin's telling he practiced this patiently, recovered over time, and went on to teach it to his own students. Readers differ about the story.
Some take the hermit at face value; others think Hakuin shaped the account to make a teaching memorable.
Either way, his point is plain: strain for awakening with only your head, and the body pays.
Bring the warmth back down. One honest note: this is a meditation, not a medical treatment. Hakuin's lesson is about balance in practice.

how: Some Zen teachers pass on Hakuin's soft-butter method and his practice of settling attention in the lower belly, especially for students who are tense or overstraining, and people read his account in Idle Talk on a Night Boat.

o: a breathing drill to sit longer without moving
an herbal medicine Hakuin made for monks who fell ill
the soft-butter meditation Hakuin learned from a hermit

p: a burning head and icy legs from straining
the hermit in a mountain cave
melts from the crown to the feet

the trouble was that he'd pushed everything up into his head.
in the meditation, the butter melts from the crown of the head down to the feet
soothing everything it touches on the way.

games.q: you're Hakuin: burning head, icy legs, no rest. the doctors can't help. what do you do?
o: go find the hermit Hakuyu in the mountains
games.why: in his telling, Hakuin sought out the hermit, who taught him to bring the energy down and melt the butter.

practice: Sit or lie down comfortably, let the breath settle low in the belly, and picture something soft and warm resting on the top of your head: butter, as Hakuyu said, or warm honey, or sunlight, whatever feels kind.
Let it slowly melt over the forehead and jaw, the shoulders, chest and belly, down the legs to the feet, taking its time wherever it meets tightness. Then rest in the warmth that's left.

wordCard.voice: Hakuin's cure. The soft-butter meditation he says he learned from the hermit Hakuyu, bringing warmth and attention down from the head to the feet. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese nanso: soft butter, the name of Hakuin's melting meditation.

carryVoice: Your line: the butter melts. Warmth, brought back down from the head. Rest well.
